title: Check a car seat belt locks: draw the webbing out slowly, jerk it so the retractor locks and holds, then ease it back
instruction: Check the seat belt: hold its latch tongue and pull the webbing out slowly, at least 12 cm, then jerk it so the belt locks, keep pulling for a second to show it holds, then let the webbing wind back in slowly until the tongue rests on its stop, and let go.
context: Almost every adult knows both halves of this from buckling up: pull a seat belt out slowly and it runs free; pull it sharply and it locks. Owner's manuals give it as the check that a belt works: "With the webbing half unreeled, hold the tongue plate and pull forward quickly. The mechanism should lock automatically and prevent further unreeling." The belt's emergency-locking retractor senses how fast the webbing speeds up: under FMVSS 209 a webbing-sensitive retractor must not lock at 0.3 g or less and must lock within 25 mm at 0.7 g. So the robot has to do two opposite things with the same grip: draw the webbing out smoothly enough that it never catches, then give a sharp jerk and keep pulling so the lock visibly takes the load, and finally let the spring take the webbing back without letting the tongue fly into the trim.
setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights are above the bench top. Stand (made for the trial, standing in for the car's door pillar and its trim): a closed grey-painted steel box 300 mm deep, 200 mm wide and 225 mm tall, bolted to the bench in front of the right arm, its face toward the robot at x = 0.355, centred on y = -0.250 (it spans x 0.355 to 0.655, y -0.350 to -0.150). On the face, a black moulded plastic trim 70 mm wide and 22 mm tall frames the belt's webbing slot, centred 155 mm above the bench. Seat belt: a car three-point seat belt with a webbing-sensitive emergency-locking retractor certified to FMVSS 209 (such as Wesco Performance's 3-point retractable belt), its retractor bolted inside the box; only the shoulder webbing and its latch tongue are used. The webbing, black-grey woven polyester 47.6 mm (1-7/8 in) wide and 1.2 mm thick, comes out of the slot level, toward the robot. A grey plastic stop button (10 x 16 x 7 mm) on the webbing keeps the tongue just outside the slot at rest. Latch tongue: a black moulded plastic body 60 mm wide, 40 mm tall and 12 mm thick with the steel tongue below it (26 mm wide, 30 mm long, 2.5 mm thick), 45 g in all; it hangs on the webbing, its top (where the webbing loops through it) at (0.310, -0.250), 155 mm up, its steel tip 80 mm above the bench. The retractor winds the webbing back in with about 2.5 N at the stop (2.9 N at 135 mm out) and locks when the webbing is pulled out sharply. Arms: both start in the raised ready pose with the fingers open; the left arm is not needed.
scoring: Measured from the start of the run (the record is cleared only at reset). Payout: how far the webbing is out of the slot beyond its rest, read off 5 mm ticks printed on it at the slot. Tension: the pull along the webbing. Jerk onset: the moment the tongue's outward acceleration rises through 0.3 g (FMVSS 209's no-lock level), from its tracked position over 20 ms windows. Stages, in order: 0.25 when the webbing has paid out at least 120 mm without locking since it last left its stop; 0.5 when a jerk then locks it within 25 mm of payout after the jerk's onset (FMVSS 209's limit) and the locked belt then carries at least 6 N for 0.25 s (twice its 2.9 N wind-back force, so an unlocked belt would pay out; the jolt of the catch alone lasts about 0.1 s) with the tongue still held; 0.75 when, after that, it carries at least 6 N for a further 1.0 s while paying out no more than 5 mm more; 1.0 when the lock is then freed and the webbing winds back to its stop (within 3 mm) never faster than 0.5 m/s (the tongue is guided in, not let fly), the tongue is let go, and both grippers are at least 30 mm clear of it and the webbing is still, for 1 s. Anything less scores 0. A jerk that never locks the belt, or a lock the hand does not keep pulling against (stopping dead where it caught), stays at 0.25; locking it during the slow pull scores 0 until the webbing is wound back to its stop and pulled out slowly again. Real trial: a 240 fps video from above with a steel rule beside the webbing gives payout, speed, the jerk's onset and the catch point; tension comes from the arm's joint-torque log, checked once against a 0-20 N spring scale hooked in the tongue's latch window while the belt is locked.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Let the webbing wind fully in until the stop button meets the trim and the tongue hangs still. Before each session check the belt by hand: a slow pull of 150 mm runs free and a sharp tug locks it; let it back a little to free the lock, and check the wind-back force with a spring scale (about 2.5 to 3 N).
fidelity: The lock is a rule standing in for the retractor's inertia disc and pawl: payout acceleration, filtered over 15 ms, trips it at 0.5 g (between FMVSS 209's 0.3 g no-lock and 0.7 g lock levels; the real setting is unpublished); the pawl catches 5 mm later; locked webbing is a 5,000 N/m spring; 2 mm let back frees it. The webbing is a rigid strip sliding through a swivel at the slot, its tail hidden in the stand. Wind-back force, drag, spool inertia, tongue size and mass are estimates.
